claims.text: The initial near-equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles have a uniform distribution of constituent elements.
Differences in constituent-element surface energies drive selective surface segregation during high-temperature operation.
Selective surface segregation produces an element-enriched passivating layer.
The passivating enriched layer stabilizes the nanoparticle structure.
The segregated surface layer modulates catalytic activity.
Controlled inert and mildly reactive atmospheres can respectively promote or suppress surface segregation during heat treatment.
Elements with lower surface energies preferentially migrate to the nanoparticle surface at service temperatures.
Formation of the segregated passivating layer reduces the nanoparticle's overall free energy.
The segregated layer protects the nanoparticle core against structural degradation.
Segregation-induced changes in surface composition alter thermoelectric properties.
High-temperature treatment in an inert atmosphere produces a detectable surface layer enriched in lower-surface-energy elements.
Reactive atmospheres make segregation less pronounced or disrupt the segregated layer.
Nanoparticles bearing the enriched layer have improved structural and chemical stability relative to untreated or reactive-atmosphere samples.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily when constituent elements have significant differences in surface energy.
The mechanism is limited when constituent elements have little variation in surface energy.
Strong chemical reactivity can overwhelm segregation kinetics and limit the proposed mechanism.
